headline: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 adds Real World AI Stage featuring robots, automated factories, and de-extinction
summary: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 is expanding its AI focus with a new stage dedicated to the intersection of digital and physical AI, exploring autonomous hardware, defense tech, and even de-extinction.
details: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 will feature a brand-new "Real World AI Stage," expanding on its previous AI programming. This stage will focus on the blending of digital and physical AI, showcasing autonomous hardware beyond self-driving cars.

The lineup includes leaders from Shield AI, Colossal Biosciences, and FieldAI. Topics will cover safely deploying autonomous vehicles, defense technologies, and industrial systems where failure has significant consequences.

Ben Lamm, CEO of Colossal Biosciences, will discuss de-extinction technologies and the role of AI in modern biology. This session will also delve into the ethical debates surrounding engineering nature for conservation.

Other sessions will explore making AI work at the edge, addressing challenges like latency and limited connectivity in defense, space, and industrial applications. Founders will share practical lessons on architectural principles and trade-offs.

The conference will also address the critical gap between prototype and scaled business for deep tech startups. Speakers from space hardware, humanoid robotics, and autonomous systems will share insights on navigating production and manufacturing realities.
TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 takes place from October 13 to 15 in San Francisco at Moscone West. Attendees can expect three days of insights, networking, and access to all stages and the exhibition floor.

headline_marked: [[Microsoft wants Xbox Helix]] to play every Xbox game ever made
headline: Microsoft wants Xbox Helix to play every Xbox game ever made
summary: A new report suggests Microsoft is aiming for unprecedented backwards compatibility on its next-gen console, potentially including original Xbox and Xbox 360 titles.
details: A leaked internal memo indicates Microsoft is urging publishers to opt into a new model that would allow legacy titles from old Xbox consoles to be available on modern devices without additional effort.
This initiative follows Microsoft's recent release of four original Xbox titles on PC with an Xbox 360 emulator, fueling speculation about broader backwards compatibility.
The memo confirms that Xbox 360 backwards compatibility is in the works for 2027-28, aligning with the expected release window for the next-gen Xbox Helix console.
Microsoft is also exploring a "Program 01" to digitize physical discs, tying games to a license accessible via an Xbox account, with a public beta planned for July 2026.

For publishers, Microsoft promises to manage all engineering, emulation, certification, merchandising, and player support, allowing them to simply grant permission and retain rights, pricing, and brand control.
This approach aims to create a "modern ecosystem" with cloud saves for older games, addressing the technical challenges of emulating non-x86 based consoles like the original Xbox and Xbox 360.
The goal is to create the largest game library on a console ever, potentially encompassing PC games and multiple generations of Xbox titles, including those requiring emulators or disc digitization.
caption:
Microsoft is reportedly pushing for the next-gen Xbox Helix to play every Xbox game ever made, from original Xbox to Xbox 360 titles.

A leaked internal memo indicates Microsoft is urging publishers to opt into a new model that would allow legacy titles from old Xbox consoles to be available on modern devices without additional effort.

This initiative follows Microsoft's recent release of four original Xbox titles on PC with an Xbox 360 emulator, fueling speculation about broader backwards compatibility.

The memo confirms that Xbox 360 backwards compatibility is in the works for 2027-28, aligning with the expected release window for the next-gen Xbox Helix console.

Microsoft is also exploring a "Program 01" to digitize physical discs, tying games to a license accessible via an Xbox account, with a public beta planned for July 2026.

For publishers, Microsoft promises to manage all engineering, emulation, certification, merchandising, and player support, allowing them to simply grant permission and retain rights, pricing, and brand control.

This approach aims to create a "modern ecosystem" with cloud saves for older games, addressing the technical challenges of emulating non-x86 based consoles like the original Xbox and Xbox 360.

The goal is to create the largest game library on a console ever, potentially encompassing PC games and multiple generations of Xbox titles, including those requiring emulators or disc digitization.
